Rhodium-Catalyzed Intermolecular Stereoselective Allylation of
Indoles with Allenes
Chaoyan Ma, Can Li, Jiahui Bai, Junzhe Xiao, Yizhan Zhai,* Yinlong Guo,* and Shengming Ma*
Cite This: ACS Catal. 2022, 12, 10141−10146
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A rhodium-catalyzed C−H functionalization-based
intermolecular allylation of indoles with trisubstituted allenes has
been developed. This synthetic process proceeds with an excellent
regioselectivity, Z-selectivity, high efficiency of chirality transfer, and a
wide tolerance of reactive functional groups under mild conditions.
Late-stage modification on a series of complex bioactive or drug
molecules and various synthetic transformations has been demonstrated. A reaction mechanism has been proposed on the basis of
mechanistic experiments and SAESI-MS studies.
KEYWORDS: indoles, allenes, allylation, rhodium-catalysis, chirality transfer, Z-selectivity
I
ndoles are intriguing and fundamental structural motifs in
numerous natural products and pharmaceuticals.
1
With
different transformations of indoles, new C−C and C−X
bonds could be selectively constructed at 2, 3, or 7 positions,
2
providing an important route to diverse structures. 2-Allylated
indoles are of current interest due to the synthetic and biological
potentials.
3
However, there is a challenge for the allylation at the
C-2 position of indoles: it could be completed by S
N
2′-type
reactions with allylic derivatives with E/Z stereoselectivity
unsolved or direct C-2 allylation (Scheme 1a).
4,5
In addition, no
asymmetric allylation has been reported with the indole
derivatives. We reasoned that allenes may be applied for such
a purpose. In principle, allenes would react with R−M mostly to
afford the π-allylic metal intermediate Int 1−1 (Scheme 1b,
top).
6
For allylation reaction with allenes, however, the
regioselectivity of the insertion step has to be reversed to the
noncommon way to produce alkenyl metal intermediates Int 1−
3 ∼ Int 1−6 (Scheme 1b, middle).
6b,c,7
So far, such a
regioselectivity switch has not been observed with the indole
derivatives. The challenges would be (1) selective formations of
Int 1−3 ∼ Int 1−6; (2) the protodemetalation of the C−M
bonds in Int 1−3 ∼ Int 1−6; and (3) the stereoselectivity
referring to the remaining C�C bond and chirality transfer of
optically active allenes fulfilling the allene-based asymmetric
allylation. Here, we wish to report rhodium-catalyzed asym-
metric allylation of indoles with trisubstituted allenes (Scheme
1b, bottom).
We began our exploration by evaluating the allylation reaction
between indole derivatives 1a-d with different directing groups
and allene 2a

To evaluate the generality of this reaction, we began to explore
the scope of trisubstituted allenes 2 with indole derivatives 1
(Table 2). First, the scope of indoles was demonstrated with 4,4-
pentamethylene-2,3-butadienyl methyl carbonate 2a: in addi-
tion to the inert 5-Me and 3-Me, synthetically versatile 5-MeO,
5-BnO, 5-Cl, 6-F, 6-Br, 4-CO
2
Me, 3-CHO, and 7-Cl could be
tolerated regardless of the electronic difference affording the
corresponding products 3ea−3na. Notably, the indoles with 3-
position substitution of 3-Me (1l) and 3-CHO (1m) increasing
the steric hindrance also worked. The scope of trisubstituted
allenes with various functional groups was also tested: the 3-
position of the allenes may be substituted with a six- to eight-
membered ring and adamantine. TBS ether, phthalimide, n-
butyl, acetate, benzoate, and an allyl ether group may all be
accommodated (3db−3dg). The reaction of a substrate bearing
acid-sensitive functional groups such as cyclic carbamate 2h and
ketal 2i also worked smoothly under the standard reaction
conditions, providing related products 3dh and 3di. The
reaction could be extended to the acyclic system, such as 4,4-
dibenzyl substitution together with piperonate unit 2j, giving the
corresponding 3dj at 70 °C.
Furthermore, the reactions with nonsymmetric trisubstituted
and optically active allenes were carried out under the standard
conditions (Scheme 2). Nonsymmetric allene 2k afforded Z-
3dk with an excellent Z-stereoselectivity. In addition, when the
optically active allenes (R)-2v, (S)-2l (S)-2m, and (R)-2l were
employed, high efficiency of chirality transfer could be achieved,
giving (S)-Z-3dv, (R)-Z-3dl, (R)-Z-3dm, and (S)-Z-3dl with
retention of the ee value in decent yields and an excellent Z
selectivity. The absolute configurations of (S)-Z-3dl and (R)-2l′
have been established by X-ray diffraction study, which
demonstrated the steric outcome of this reaction. Similarly,

when the optically active compounds (S)-2w (99% ee), (R)-2n
(99% ee), and (S)-2n (99% ee) were applied, (R)-Z-3dw (99%
ee), (S)-Z-3dn (99% ee), and (R)-Z-3dn (99% ee) could be
obtained, respectively, with a Z/E-selectivity of 73:27 to 88:12
and an excellent level of efficient chirality transfer. In addition,
employing optically active 1,3-disubstituted allene (R)-2x could
not afford the desired product.
Moreover, some other type substrates were also attempted
(Scheme 3): the reaction of 1,1-disubstituted allene 2y could
afford 3dy in a yield of 74%, whereas no allylation product could
be detected for the monosubstituted allene 2z and 1,3-
disubstituted allene 2x. To our delight, when pyrrole derivative
1o was applied with 2a, it also successfully gave the desired
product 3oa in 83% yield.
To demonstrate the synthetic utility and practicality of the
method, a series of synthetic applications was carried out. Firstly,
a gram-scale reaction of 3 mmol scale was conducted, which
afforded 1.25 g (91% yield) of 3ho (Scheme 4a). Next,
trisubstituted allenes bearing units from natural products or drug
molecules were synthesized according to the ATA
7b
reaction
and esterification. Under the standard conditions, a range of
cyclic and acyclic trisubstituted allenes derivatized from (1S)-
(−)-camphanicacid (5), adapalene (6), cholesteryl hemi-
succinate (7), indometacin (8), fenofibrate acid (9), isoxepac
(10), oxaprozin (17), and febuxostat (18) are compatible,
affording the related products 3dp−3dB in decent yields and
complete Z-stereoselectivity for compound 3du (Scheme 4b).
Furthermore, such products are synthetically versatile: when
indole product 3dd was treated with NaOEt and DMSO at 110
°C, the directing group could be removed to generate
corresponding indole 11.
9
Next, homoallyl alcohol compound
12 could be yielded by reacting with TBAF·3H
2
O; compound
13 could be formed with phenylacetylene via Pd-catalyzed
Sonogashira coupling reaction.
10
2-Pyrimidinyl may be further
applied to implement C−H functionalization at C-7 of indole
with methyl acrylate to afford compound 14.
11
Suzuki coupling
reaction of (R)-3dm with PhB(OH)
2
could generate compound
15
12
without racemization. Phthalimide could be removed and
the subsequent reaction with tosyl chloride afforded tosyl amide
16 without racemization (Scheme 4c).
In order to gain insight into the reaction mechanism, a series
of deuterium-labeling and control experiments were conducted
(Scheme 5). First, approximately 26% deuterium incorporation
was observed at the 2-position of 1d when the reaction of 1d was
conducted with 1 equiv of PivOD in the absence of 2a,
indicating that the C−H bond activation process is reversible
(Scheme 5, eq 1). Next, the reaction of 1d with 2a was
conducted with 1 equiv of PivOD under the standard
conditions; a 38% deuterium incorporation onto the olefinic
position of product 3da was observed (Scheme 5, eq 2).
Moreover, under otherwise identical conditions, the reaction
employing 1d-D1 with D incorporation of 96% at the 2-position
with 2a afforded the product 3da-D1 with 56% and 20%
deuterium incorporation at the vinylic position 7-position of the
indole moiety, respectively (Scheme 5, eq 3). A control
experiment using 1d-D1 and PivOH led to a decrease of
deuterium incorporation at the vinylic position (Scheme 5, eq
4). These experiments indicated that olefinic hydrogen
originated from the proton of PivOH and the 2-position of
1d. The kinetic isotope effect was determined by using 1d and
1d-D1 via parallel and competitive experiments to be 1.00 and
1.15 based on the integration of indole C3 H NMR analysis,
indicating that the C−H activation is not the rate-determining
step (Scheme 5, eqs 5−7). Moreover, to verify the possibility for
C-7 allylation, two experiments were conducted: when
increasing the amount of 2a and prolonging the reaction time,
the allylation at C-7 could not be achieved (Scheme 5, eq 8); the
reaction of product 3da with 1.1 equiv. of 2a under the standard
conditions still failed to afford the product functionalized at the
C-7 position (Scheme 5, eq 9). Thus, the C−H allylation
occurred exclusively at the 2-position.

spectrometric experiment (SAESI-MS) was conducted to detect

2-pyrimidinyl as the directing group. Subsequently, trisubsti-
tuted allene 2 undergoes a highly regioselective syn-insertion
with the C−Rh bond in Int 2−1, leading to the formation of Int
2−2 supported by the detection of MS-Int-2.
Subsequent protonation of Int 2−2 or Int 2−3 afforded
corresponding product (R)-Z-3 or (S)-E-3′, followed by
releasing the rhodium catalyst to finish the catalytic cycle.
Obviously, the Z-stereoselectiovity may be rationalized by the
fact that Int 2−3 is disfavored owing to steric hindrance. The
efficiency of chirality transfer may be explained by the strict syn-
insertion and stereospecific protodemetaltion.
In conclusion, we have developed a novel rhodium-catalyzed
asymmetric C−H allylation of indoles with trisubstituted allenes
under mild conditions. The overall process exhibits excellent
atom economy, unique regioselectivity and stereoselectivity, and
good functional group tolerance. Synthetic applications as well
as the mechanistic investigation have been conducted and
enhanced the utility and understanding of the reaction.
